summary: A 1971 proposal for NETRJS, a third-level protocol for Remote Job Entry, by R. T. Braden and S. M. Wolfe. Remote job entry lets users submit batch jobs to a distant computer. It was replaced by RFC 189.

eli5.summary: A way to send work to a big computer far away and get the results back. A newer note replaced it.

questions: how to submit batch jobs over the arpanet
subtitle: A way for remote users to run batch jobs on a distant computer.

tldr.problem: Users wanted to submit batch jobs to a central computer (like an IBM System/360) from across the ARPA Network, as if they were using a remote card reader, printer, and punch card device.
tldr.mechanism: NETRJS defines a third-level protocol layered over the Network Control Program. It simulates physical device channels (card reader for input, printer and punch for output) and opens separate network connections for each simulated device, plus operator console channels for messages.
tldr.outcome: The protocol enabled users to submit jobs and retrieve output over the network, but was soon replaced by more general file transfer and job submission protocols.

facts.label: Device types
facts.value: 5 standard (operator input, operator output, card reader, printer, punch)

today: RFC 88 describes a 1971 protocol that was replaced almost immediately by RFC 189, a more complete NETRJS specification. The approach of device simulation gave way to more general network file transfer and job submission protocols.

sections.title: Remote Job Entry Over the Network
sections.content:
NETRJS (Network Remote Job Service) is a protocol that lets a user at a remote host submit batch jobs to the RJS (Remote Job Service) system at a central site, usually an IBM System/360 computer. The remote user's process simulates a physical remote batch terminal, complete with a card reader for submitting jobs and a printer and card punch for receiving output.

The protocol supports multiple simultaneous users at the same remote host, each identified by an 8-character terminal ID, each with their own set of virtual devices.
sections.eli5: A program that acts like a remote terminal connected to a big mainframe, so you can submit work and get results back over the network.

sections.title: Channels and Device Simulation
sections.content:
NETRJS opens separate network connections called channels for each simulated device. A standard remote site has five channels: operator input (for commands), operator output (for system messages), a simulated card reader (input stream for job submission), a printer (output for printed results), and a card punch (output for binary or punched card data).

Each device channel becomes open only when needed. Data flows as variable-length blocks up to 900 bytes (operator channels limited to 130 bytes). Block format includes a header with a control byte, optional checksum, and device identification, followed by variable-length records of data.
sections.eli5: Each virtual device (card reader, printer, punch) gets its own connection to the remote computer. Data goes in blocks, like envelopes full of punched cards.

sections.title: Starting and Ending Sessions
sections.content:
A remote user begins by sending an initial RFC (Request For Connection) to the central site's incoming logger. The logger allocates a set of socket numbers and returns them, allowing the remote site to open the operator input channel. The remote user then sends a SIGNON message with their terminal ID. If RJS recognizes the ID, it proceeds; otherwise, it closes the connection.

To end the session, the user sends a SIGNOFF command, and RJS waits for current job output to complete before closing the operator output channel. If either site encounters a fatal error, it closes all channels for that session.
sections.eli5: To start, you say hello with your terminal name. When you're done, you say goodbye. The system cleans up everything when the connection ends.
